q: A business partner ends its contract because the company failed a required security audit. What consequence is this?
w: Non-compliance can break or end contracts.
h: Fail the audit, lose the deal.

q: The company files a required compliance report with its regulator. What type of reporting is this?
w: Reporting to regulators or outside parties is external.
h: Outside eyes = external reporting.

q: A tool checks control settings continuously and alerts when something falls out of compliance. What is this?
w: Automation catches drift between audits.
h: Check all the time, not once a year.

q: Management formally affirms that required controls are in place and working. What is this?
w: Attestation is a formal statement that controls are in place.
h: Attest = officially vouch.

q: A regulator restricts the organization from certain activities as a penalty. What consequence is this?
w: Sanctions are imposed restrictions or penalties.
h: Sanctions put limits on what you can do.

q: After a public breach, members move their accounts to competitors. What consequence is this?
w: Lost trust drives customers away.
h: Trust lost is customers lost.

q: A credit union only accepts card payments through a third-party processor and never stores card numbers. Does PCI DSS still apply?
o: Yes, but scope can be reduced
Only if it has more than 1,000 members
w: Any organization accepting cards has PCI obligations; outsourcing reduces scope.
h: Taking cards means PCI applies, even if lightly.

q: The help desk gets calls from 40 users who are all locked out within the same 10 minutes. Which indicator is this?
w: A wave of lockouts suggests brute-force or password-spraying activity.
h: Many lockouts at once = someone is guessing.

q: Logs show backup jobs running at 2 PM instead of the usual 2 AM, with no change ticket. Which indicator is this?
w: Activity at unexpected times, outside the normal cycle, is suspicious.
h: Right job, wrong time.

q: The domain controller's Security log has no entries between 01:00 and 01:40, though the server was running. Which indicator is this?
w: Gaps in logs often mean an attacker deleted or stopped logging.
h: Silence in the logs is suspicious.

q: Users suddenly can't open files on a share, and the files now end in ".locked". Which indicator is this?
w: Data or systems that can't be reached are an indicator, here pointing to ransomware.
h: Suddenly locked out of your own stuff.

q: A workstation sends 30 GB of outbound traffic overnight when it normally sends a few hundred MB. Which indicator is this?
w: Unusual bandwidth, CPU, or disk use can point to exfiltration or mining.
h: Usage spikes tell stories.

q: Proxy logs show one host repeatedly trying to reach a domain the web filter blocks as malware. Which indicator is this?
w: Repeated blocked requests suggest malware trying to call home.
h: The filter keeps saying no to the same host.

q: Your credit union's member data shows up for sale on a criminal leak site. Which indicator is this?
w: Data appearing publicly is a direct indicator of compromise.
h: If it's for sale, it was stolen.

q: A user signs in from Chicago, then from Tokyo 20 minutes later. Which indicator is this?
w: The distance can't be traveled in the time between logins.
h: No one flies to Tokyo in 20 minutes.

q: The same VPN account is active from two different IP addresses at the same moment. Which indicator is this?
w: One account active in two places at once suggests shared or stolen credentials.
h: One person, two places, same time.

q: The firewall shows connections to an IP that your threat feed lists as a known command-and-control server. What is this an example of?
w: A known-bad IP, hash, or domain seen in your environment is an IOC.
h: IOC = evidence the bad guy was here.

q: A single domain admin account is locked out repeatedly by failed logins coming from many different IPs. What is MOST likely happening?
o: A user who forgot a new password
w: Repeated failures from many sources against one privileged account point to an attack.
h: Many hands rattling one important door.

q: What does Windows Event ID 1102 indicate?
o: The security audit log was cleared
w: Clearing the log is a classic sign of covering tracks.
h: 1102 = someone wiped the logs.

q: A server's CPU and disk run at 100% overnight with no scheduled jobs. Which indicator is this?
w: Unexplained resource use can mean cryptomining, encryption, or data staging.
h: Busy with nothing scheduled = suspicious.

q: A user reports their password stopped working, and logs show it was changed from an unfamiliar IP. What is this MOST likely evidence of?
w: An unexpected password change from an unknown location suggests a compromised account.
h: Someone changed your locks.

q: Which indicator BEST suggests an attacker is trying to hide their activity?
o: A spike in help desk tickets
A new printer on the network
w: Attackers delete logs to cover their tracks.
h: Erased footprints mean someone was walking.

q: Logs show a service account logging in interactively at a workstation, which it has never done before. What should this be treated as?
w: Service accounts shouldn't log on interactively; deviation from baseline is suspicious.
h: When a robot starts acting like a person, look closer.

q: EDR alerts that antivirus was disabled on 30 workstations at the same time. What should this be treated as?
o: A likely sign of an attack in progress
A false positive until proven otherwise
w: Mass disabling of security tools often precedes ransomware deployment.
h: Attackers switch off the alarms first.

q: What happens to traffic from 10.0.5.20 to 52.1.1.1 on TCP 443?
c:
1  PERMIT  TCP  10.0.5.0/24  any  443
2  DENY    TCP  any          any  443 (log)
3  DENY    IP   any          any  any (log)
w: 10.0.5.20 is in 10.0.5.0/24, so rule 1 matches first.
h: First match wins.

q: Same rules: what happens to traffic from 10.0.6.20 to 52.1.1.1 on TCP 443?
c:
1  PERMIT  TCP  10.0.5.0/24  any  443
2  DENY    TCP  any          any  443 (log)
3  DENY    IP   any          any  any (log)
w: 10.0.6.20 isn't in 10.0.5.0/24, so rule 1 doesn't match; rule 2 does.
h: Check the subnet before the port.

q: Same rules: what happens to traffic from 10.0.5.20 to 52.1.1.1 on TCP 80?
c:
1  PERMIT  TCP  10.0.5.0/24  any  443
2  DENY    TCP  any          any  443 (log)
3  DENY    IP   any          any  any (log)
w: Port 80 doesn't match rules 1 or 2, so it falls to the final deny.
h: Every field must match, port included.

q: What happens to SSH from 192.168.10.50 to 10.1.1.10?
c:
1  DENY    TCP  192.168.10.50    any        22
2  PERMIT  TCP  192.168.10.0/24  10.1.1.10  22
3  DENY    IP   any              any        any
w: The specific deny sits above the broad permit, so it matches first.
h: Specific above broad works.

q: Same rules: what happens to SSH from 192.168.10.60 to 10.1.1.10?
c:
1  DENY    TCP  192.168.10.50    any        22
2  PERMIT  TCP  192.168.10.0/24  10.1.1.10  22
3  DENY    IP   any              any        any
w: .60 doesn't match rule 1's single host, so rule 2 permits it.
h: Rule 1 only names one host.

q: Same rules: what happens to SSH from 192.168.10.60 to 10.1.1.11?
c:
1  DENY    TCP  192.168.10.50    any        22
2  PERMIT  TCP  192.168.10.0/24  10.1.1.10  22
3  DENY    IP   any              any        any
w: Rule 2 only permits destination 10.1.1.10, so .11 falls to the deny.
h: Destination must match too.

q: Which rule never takes effect?
c:
1  PERMIT  TCP  any  172.20.0.0/16  any
2  DENY    TCP  any  172.20.5.5     3389
o: Rule 2, because rule 1 matches that traffic first
Rule 1, because rule 2 is more specific
w: A broad permit above a specific deny shadows the deny.
h: The broad rule above hides the one below.

q: A firewall permits UDP 53 to the DNS server, but zone transfers and large responses fail. What's missing?
w: DNS uses TCP 53 for zone transfers and large responses.
h: DNS speaks UDP mostly, TCP when it's big.

q: Only outbound rules exist for web browsing, yet reply traffic gets back in. Why?
o: The firewall is stateful and tracks connections
There is an implicit allow for inbound traffic
Port 443 is open in both directions by default
The firewall is stateless and allows replies
w: Stateful firewalls track sessions and permit their replies.
h: Stateful remembers who called.

q: Rule 1 is "PERMIT IP any any any." What effect does it have on all the rules below it?
o: Every rule below it is shadowed
Only deny rules below it still apply
The rules below it are checked first
It applies to UDP traffic only
w: The first rule matches everything, so processing never reaches the rest.
h: An open door at the top makes the rest of the list pointless.

q: Which rule BEST lets only the HR subnet 10.10.30.0/24 reach the payroll server 10.10.20.15 on HTTPS?
w: Least privilege means the narrowest source, destination, and port.
h: Narrow on every field.

q: Why add an explicit "DENY IP any any any (log)" at the bottom when implicit deny already exists?
w: The explicit rule creates a record of what was blocked.
h: Implicit deny blocks silently; explicit deny takes notes.

q: How should a specific deny and an overlapping broad permit be ordered?
o: Specific deny first, broad permit after
Broad permit first, specific deny after
w: With first-match processing, specific rules must come before broad ones.
h: VIPs and banned people go at the top.

q: Which rule BEST stops workstations on 10.0.0.0/8 from sending SMB to the internet?
o: DENY TCP any 10.0.0.0/8 445, at the bottom
w: Outbound SMB must be denied by source before broad permits match it.
h: Block it on the way out, and put it high.

q: What does this rule allow?
w: Source any, destination the mail server, port 25 means mail can be delivered to it.
h: Read it as "from, to, on which port."

q: A rule permits TCP 3389 from "any" to 10.3.3.0/24. What is the main risk?
o: RDP on that subnet is reachable from anywhere
Only outbound RDP from the subnet is allowed
Nothing, because RDP traffic is encrypted
Only hosts inside 10.3.3.0/24 can use RDP
w: A source of "any" opens RDP to the whole internet if this is the edge firewall.
h: "Any" in the source means everyone.

q: In Windows Defender Firewall, an allow rule and a block rule both match the same traffic. What usually happens?
w: Windows Firewall doesn't use top-down order; block rules generally take precedence.
h: In Windows Firewall, block beats allow.

q: EDR shows "wbadmin delete catalog -quiet" on a file server at 3 AM. What is the attacker MOST likely doing?
w: Deleting the backup catalog removes Windows backup restores, just like deleting shadow copies.
h: Burn the spare keys before locking the house.

q: EDR shows "wevtutil cl Security" right after an attacker's logon. What is the purpose?
w: wevtutil cl clears event logs to hide activity.
h: Wipe the footprints.

q: rclone uploads 60 GB to cloud storage an hour before file encryption begins. What tactic is this?
w: Attackers steal data first so they can threaten to leak it.
h: Steal it, then lock it.

q: What does "double extortion" ransomware mean?
o: Encrypt the data and threaten to leak it
Demand two payments for the same key
Have two ransomware groups attack at once
Double the ransom every day it's unpaid
w: Theft plus encryption gives two forms of pressure.
h: Pay to unlock, and pay to keep it quiet.

q: Ransomware is actively spreading across file servers at 2 AM. What should be done FIRST?
w: Containment stops the spread before recovery begins.
h: Stop the spread before cleaning up.

q: Why avoid powering off a ransomware-infected server during the incident?
o: It destroys volatile evidence in memory
It speeds up encryption on the disk
It deletes the server's local backups
It alerts the attacker's C2 server
w: RAM can hold keys, processes, and attacker tools; isolation keeps it intact.
h: Unplug the network, not the power.

q: How do investigators identify "patient zero" in a ransomware incident?
o: Find the earliest compromised host in the timeline
Pick the server with the most encrypted files
Pick the host with the ransom note
w: Patient zero is where the attack started, found by tracing back the timeline.
h: Follow the timeline to the first domino.

q: What does the 3-2-1 backup rule require?
o: Three copies, on two media types, with one offsite
Three backups a day, two weekly, one monthly
Three servers, two sites, one cloud
Three admins, two keys, one vault
w: Keeping copies separated protects against ransomware and site loss.
h: 3 copies, 2 media, 1 offsite.

q: What makes a backup "immutable"?
o: It can't be changed or deleted for a set period
It's encrypted with AES-256 at rest
It's stored on the same server as the data
It's compressed to save storage space
w: Immutable backups survive attackers with admin rights.
h: Written once, can't be erased.

q: Before restoring servers from backup after ransomware, what must be done?
o: Confirm backups are clean and close the entry point
Pay the ransom so the attackers leave quietly
Delete all logs to free space for the restore
Re-enable the compromised accounts for staff
w: Restoring onto a still-open hole or from infected backups leads to reinfection.
h: Fix the door before moving back in.

q: Why can paying a ransom create legal risk for a U.S. organization?
o: The payment may go to a sanctioned group (OFAC)
It's required by law to report payments to the attacker
w: Paying sanctioned entities can violate Treasury rules.
h: Paying the wrong group can break federal law.

q: Ransomware entered when a user enabled macros in an emailed document. Which control BEST prevents this path?
o: Block macros in internet Office files
Require longer passwords for all users
Disable DNS logging on the endpoints
Pause Windows Update during business hours
w: Blocking internet macros cuts a common initial access route.
h: No macros from strangers.

q: EDR shows PsExec launching the same binary on 50 servers from one admin workstation. What stage is this?
w: Remote execution tools spreading a payload across hosts show lateral movement.
h: One machine pushing to many = spreading.

q: Ransomware was deployed to every workstation through a new Group Policy Object. What does this tell you?
o: An account that can edit Group Policy was compromised
Only a standard user account was compromised
w: Creating domain-wide GPOs requires high privileges such as Domain Admin.
h: GPO deployment means the attacker had the keys to the kingdom.

q: Which team should be engaged early in a ransomware incident because of breach-notification laws?
w: Legal determines notification duties and deadlines.
h: Call the lawyers early.

q: Which systems should be restored first after ransomware?
o: The ones with the shortest RTO in the BIA
The servers that were encrypted last
The ones with the most user complaints
The systems with the newest hardware
w: Recovery priorities come from the business impact analysis.
h: Restore what the business needs most, first.

q: Lessons learned shows EDR alerted but no one responded for 6 hours overnight. What is the BEST improvement?
o: Buy a second EDR product for overlap
Delete older alerts to reduce noise
Turn off overnight logging to save cost
w: Detection without response doesn't stop ransomware.
h: An alarm nobody hears doesn't help.

q: In IaaS, who is responsible for patching the guest operating system?
w: In IaaS, the customer manages the OS and everything above it.
h: IaaS: you rent the hardware, you run the OS.

q: In SaaS, what is the customer still responsible for?
w: The provider runs the app; the customer controls who uses it and what goes in.
h: SaaS: you bring the users and data.

q: In PaaS, what does the customer manage?
o: The guest OS and its patches
w: PaaS provides the runtime; the customer builds and secures the app.
h: PaaS: you bring the code.

q: In every cloud model, who is responsible for the physical security of the data center?
w: Physical infrastructure is always the provider's job.
h: The provider guards the building.

q: A storage bucket was left publicly readable and member files were exposed. Under shared responsibility, whose fault is this?
w: Access settings on customer resources are the customer's responsibility.
h: The provider gives you the lock; you set it.

q: Many forgotten, unpatched VMs exist that no one tracks. What is this problem?
w: Untracked VMs pile up and create unmanaged risk.
h: Sprawl: VMs multiply when no one's counting.

q: Which hypervisor runs directly on the hardware with no host operating system?
w: Type 1 hypervisors like ESXi run on bare metal.
h: Type 1 = first on the metal.

q: VirtualBox runs on top of a Windows laptop's OS. What type of hypervisor is this?
w: Type 2 hypervisors run as applications on a host OS.
h: Type 2 = second layer, on top of an OS.

q: Code runs as functions only when triggered, and the provider manages all servers. What is this?
w: Serverless runs code on demand with no server management by the customer.
h: Serverless still has servers; you just don't see them.

q: Cloud environments are built from version-controlled templates instead of manual clicks. What is this, and what is its main security benefit?
w: IaC makes builds repeatable and lets security review changes like code.
h: Build it from a recipe, not from memory.

q: Which tool gives visibility and control over which SaaS apps employees use, including shadow IT?
w: A cloud access security broker sits between users and cloud services.
h: CASB watches the road to the cloud.

q: A company runs some systems on-premises and others in a public cloud, connected together. What is this?
w: Hybrid mixes on-premises and cloud.
h: Hybrid = part home, part cloud.

q: A company uses both AWS and Azure to avoid depending on a single provider. What is this?
w: Multi-cloud uses more than one cloud provider.
h: Multi = many providers.

q: Which cloud control acts as a virtual firewall attached to individual instances?
w: Security groups filter traffic at the instance or network interface.
h: Security groups are firewalls that follow the VM.

q: Container images in the registry contain outdated libraries with known CVEs. What should be done?
o: Scan images and rebuild from patched bases
Move containers to a Type 2 hypervisor
w: Image scanning catches vulnerable layers before deployment.
h: Patch the recipe, then rebake.

q: A developer committed cloud access keys to a public GitHub repo. What should be done FIRST?
o: Wait to see if they're used
w: Bots scrape public repos within minutes, so the keys must be treated as stolen.
h: Once public, assume stolen.

q: Which cloud model gives one organization an entire cloud environment dedicated only to it?
w: A private cloud serves one organization exclusively.
h: Private = yours alone.

q: A file's owner decides who else can read or change it. Which access control model is this?
w: In DAC, the owner has discretion over permissions.
h: DAC = the owner decides.

q: All tellers get the same permissions because of their job title. Which model is this?
w: Permissions tied to job roles is RBAC.
h: RBAC = permissions by job.

q: Users get only the access needed for their job, nothing more. What principle is this?
w: Least privilege limits damage from mistakes and compromises.
h: Just enough, nothing extra.

q: One employee can create new vendors, but a different employee must approve payments to them. What principle is this?
w: Splitting a sensitive process prevents one person from committing fraud alone.
h: It takes two to steal.

q: Tellers can only log in between 7 AM and 7 PM. What control is this?
w: Limiting access by time reduces risk from off-hours misuse.
h: The door only opens during business hours.

q: An employee moved from loans to marketing years ago but still has loan system access. What is this problem?
w: Permissions pile up as people change roles.
h: Permissions follow you unless someone removes them.

q: Which control BEST catches privilege creep?
w: Managers regularly confirm each user's access is still needed.
h: Review who has what, on a schedule.

q: Admins check out a domain admin password from a vault, and it's rotated after use. What is this?
w: Privileged access management vaults and rotates powerful credentials.
h: Borrow the key, return it, it changes.

q: A cloud task gets temporary credentials that expire automatically when the job finishes. What are these?
w: Short-lived credentials limit how long stolen secrets are useful.
h: Credentials that vanish on their own.

q: Users can't share classified files with anyone, even files they created, because the system enforces labels. Which model is this?
w: In MAC, the system enforces labels and users can't override them.
h: MAC: the system decides, not the owner.

q: What is the main administrative advantage of RBAC?
o: Changing someone's job means changing one role
Every user gets a unique set of permissions
File owners decide who gets access to what
It removes the need for any security groups
w: Managing roles is easier than managing individual permissions.
h: Change the role, not every permission.

q: If access isn't explicitly granted, it is denied. What is this principle?
w: Anything not allowed is blocked by default.
h: Not on the list? Not getting in.

q: Access is allowed only from managed devices in the U.S., for users in the Finance department. Which model is this?
w: Combining user, device, and location attributes is ABAC.
h: ABAC weighs many attributes at once.

q: Employees periodically switch positions, which can reveal hidden fraud. What is this control?
w: Someone new in the role may spot irregularities.
h: A fresh set of eyes finds what was hidden.

q: Employees must take at least five consecutive days off each year so someone else does their work. What is this control?
w: Fraud often surfaces when the person hiding it isn't there.
h: When they're away, the truth comes out.

q: How should a service account that runs a backup job be configured?
o: Least privilege and no interactive logon
Domain admin with a password that never changes
w: Service accounts should have only the rights their task needs.
h: A service account does one job, nothing more.

q: Why are shared accounts like "frontdesk1" a problem?
o: Actions can't be traced to one person
They can't be protected with MFA
They slow down the login process
w: Without individual accounts there's no accountability or non-repudiation.
h: If everyone is "frontdesk1," no one did it.

q: Employees' web traffic passes through a device that filters content and caches pages for them. What is it?
w: A forward proxy sits in front of users and acts on their behalf.
h: Forward proxy faces out for your users.

q: What is the main purpose of a load balancer?
o: Spread traffic for performance and availability
Encrypt traffic stored on the web servers
Assign IP addresses to the server pool
w: Load balancers distribute requests and route around failed servers.
h: Share the load so no one server drowns.

q: All three servers behind a load balancer handle traffic at the same time. What configuration is this?
w: In active-active, every node serves traffic.
h: Active-active: everyone works.

q: One server handles all traffic, and a second waits idle to take over if it fails. What configuration is this?
w: Active-passive keeps a standby ready for failover.
h: One works, one waits.

q: Which device terminates hundreds of remote-access VPN tunnels from teleworkers?
w: A VPN concentrator is built to handle many VPN connections.
h: The concentrator gathers all the tunnels.

q: A network appliance inspects outbound traffic and blocks emails containing member account numbers. What is it?
w: Data loss prevention looks for sensitive data leaving the network.
h: DLP stops data from walking out.

q: Which device BEST blocks SQL injection and XSS against a public web app?
w: A WAF inspects HTTP requests for web attacks.
h: WAF guards web apps.

q: A firewall identifies applications regardless of port and ties rules to AD users. What type is it?
w: App awareness and user identity are NGFW features.
h: NGFW knows the app and the user.

q: A small branch wants firewall, IPS, antivirus, and content filtering in one inexpensive box. What fits?
w: Unified threat management bundles many functions for small sites.
h: UTM = all-in-one for small offices.

q: A device at a remote branch collects traffic data and forwards it to the central IDS and SIEM. What is it?
w: Sensors gather data where the traffic is and send it to central analysis.
h: Sensors are the eyes in each room.

q: An IDS alerts because a server suddenly sends ten times its normal traffic, though no signature matched. Which detection method is this?
w: Anomaly detection compares activity to a learned baseline.
h: Anomaly = "this isn't normal."

q: An inline IPS starts blocking legitimate payroll traffic it mistakes for an attack. What is the main problem with IPS false positives?
w: An IPS acts on its decisions, so false positives disrupt business.
h: An IPS mistake stops real work.

q: A proxy filters users' web traffic without any browser configuration on their devices. What type is it?
w: A transparent proxy intercepts traffic without client settings.
h: Transparent: users don't know it's there.

q: Which device mainly forwards packets between networks and can apply basic access lists?
w: Routers connect networks and can filter with ACLs.
h: Routers route between networks.

q: A load balancer sends /api requests to one pool and /images to another. What type of load balancing is this?
w: Layer 7 balancers route based on application data like URL paths.
h: Layer 7 reads the URL.

q: A load balancer decrypts HTTPS so the web servers don't have to. What is this?
w: Offloading moves TLS processing to the load balancer and allows inspection.
h: Let the front door handle the locks.

q: A login requires a password and a PIN. How many authentication factors is this?
w: Two items from the same category are still one factor.
h: Two "knows" are still one factor.

q: A login requires a fingerprint and a smart card. How many factors is this?
o: Two: something you are and something you have
Two: something you know and something you have
w: Different categories make it multifactor.
h: Different kinds of proof = MFA.

q: A fingerprint scan is which authentication factor?
w: Biometrics are something you are.
h: You are your fingerprint.

q: Access is allowed only if the user's IP is inside the corporate network. Which factor is this?
w: Location is an authentication attribute.
h: Where you are can count too.

q: A biometric system lets an impostor in. Which rate measures this error?
w: FAR counts wrongly accepted people, the security risk.
h: FAR: false "yes."

q: A biometric reader keeps rejecting authorized employees. Which rate measures this?
w: FRR counts legitimate users wrongly turned away.
h: FRR: false "no."

q: What does a lower crossover error rate (CER) indicate about a biometric system?
w: CER is where FAR and FRR are equal; lower means better accuracy.
h: Lower CER, better scanner.

q: What is the difference between HOTP and TOTP codes?
o: HOTP is counter-based; TOTP is time-based
HOTP is time-based; TOTP is counter-based
w: TOTP changes every 30 seconds or so; HOTP changes with each use.
h: T for time.

q: Which password practice does current NIST guidance favor?
o: Long passwords screened against breach lists
Short complex passwords changed every 30 days
Passwords that never change and can be shared
Passwords changed whenever users choose to
w: NIST favors length and breached-password screening; forced rotation leads to weak patterns.
h: Long and unique beats short and complicated.

q: What is the main security benefit of a password manager?
o: A unique, long password for every site
No need for MFA on any account
Easy sharing of passwords with coworkers
w: Unique passwords stop one breach from unlocking other accounts.
h: One vault, many unique keys.

q: Users sign in to Windows with a device-bound key unlocked by a PIN or face. What is this?
w: Passwordless uses a key on the device plus a local gesture; there's no password to steal.
h: No password to phish.

q: In Kerberos, what does the KDC issue first so users can request access to services?
w: The TGT lets users request service tickets without re-entering their password.
h: TGT = the ticket for getting more tickets.

q: What is the main risk of single sign-on?
o: One stolen login can open many apps
Users end up with more passwords
It prevents the use of MFA
It makes every login much slower
w: SSO concentrates risk, so it should be protected with strong MFA.
h: One key opens many doors, so guard it well.

q: A government employee uses a PIV card plus a PIN to log in. What does the card represent?
w: The physical card is possession; the PIN is knowledge.
h: The card is in your pocket.

q: Attackers try one common password, like "Spring2026!", against every account. Which control BEST stops this?
w: Password spraying avoids lockouts, so MFA and banned-password lists are the fix.
h: One password, many accounts: MFA breaks it.

q: What is the purpose of a minimum password age setting?
o: Prevent cycling back to an old password
Make new passwords longer than old ones
Force MFA on every password change
Lock accounts that sit idle too long
w: Without it, users change passwords repeatedly to reuse the old one.
h: Can't spin the dial back to the old password.

q: A risk assessment rates threats as high, medium, or low instead of in dollars. What type is it?
w: Qualitative uses ratings or categories rather than numbers.
h: Qualitative = words, quantitative = dollars.

q: A risk assessment calculates expected annual losses in dollars. What type is it?
w: Quantitative assessments use numeric values like SLE and ALE.
h: Quantitative counts the money.

q: What is the formula for single loss expectancy (SLE)?
w: SLE is the cost of one occurrence.
h: SLE = AV × EF.

q: A server room flood is expected once every 4 years. What is the ARO?
w: ARO is occurrences per year: 1 ÷ 4 = 0.25.
h: Once every N years = 1/N.

q: A credit union stops offering a risky product entirely to eliminate its risk. Which treatment is this?
w: Ending the activity avoids the risk.
h: Avoid: don't do the risky thing.

q: The team adds MFA and monitoring to reduce the chance of account takeover. Which treatment is this?
w: Adding controls lowers likelihood or impact.
h: Mitigate = add controls.

q: Fixing a low risk would cost far more than the loss it could cause, so leadership documents and keeps it. Which treatment is this?
w: Acceptance is a formal decision to live with a risk.
h: Accept when the fix costs more than the loss.

q: Which document lists risks with their owners, likelihood, impact, and treatment?
w: The risk register tracks risks through their lifecycle.
h: The register is the risk to-do list.

q: Who is accountable for managing a specific risk in the register?
w: Each risk needs an owner responsible for its treatment.
h: Every risk needs a name next to it.

q: The board states the credit union will accept only minimal risk with member data. What is this describing?
w: Appetite is how much risk the organization is willing to take; conservative means little.
h: Conservative appetite = small bites of risk.

q: A startup accepts higher risk to grow quickly. What type of risk appetite is this?
w: Expansionary appetites take on more risk for growth.
h: Expansionary = willing to take big bites.

q: What is the risk that remains after controls are applied?
w: Residual risk is what's left over.
h: Residual = leftover.

q: What is the risk level before any controls are applied?
w: Inherent risk is the raw risk of the activity.
h: Inherent = built in.

q: Risks are reassessed every quarter on a fixed schedule. What type of assessment is this?
w: Recurring assessments happen at regular intervals.
h: Recurring = on the calendar.

q: SLE is $10,000 and the event happens 3 times a year. What is the ALE?
w: ALE = SLE × ARO.
h: Cost per event times events per year.

q: Risks are plotted on a grid of likelihood versus impact, colored green to red. What is this?
w: A heat map shows which risks need attention first.
h: Red corner = fix first.

q: Which recovery site is fully equipped with current data and can take over within minutes?
w: A hot site is ready to run almost immediately, at the highest cost.
h: Hot = ready now.

q: Which recovery site has space and power but no equipment or data?
w: A cold site is cheapest but slowest to bring online.
h: Cold = empty room.

q: Which recovery site has hardware ready but needs current data loaded before use?
w: A warm site is a middle ground in cost and recovery time.
h: Warm = partly ready.

q: What does a UPS mainly provide during a power outage?
o: Short-term power until a generator starts
Several days of power during an outage
Internet failover when the ISP is down
Cooling for the data center if HVAC fails
w: A UPS covers the gap; generators cover long outages.
h: UPS bridges the gap.

q: Which device keeps a data center running through a multi-day power outage?
w: Generators provide long-term power with fuel.
h: UPS for minutes, generator for days.

q: Why put the backup data center in a different region from the primary?
o: So one disaster can't take out both
w: Geographic dispersion protects against regional events.
h: Don't keep both eggs in the same storm's path.

q: Several servers work together and appear as one system; if one fails, another takes over. What is this?
w: Clustering provides high availability through failover between members.
h: Clustered servers act as one.

q: The DR site processes real transactions alongside the primary site to confirm it works. What type of test is this?
w: Parallel tests run both sites at once without stopping the primary.
h: Run both side by side.

q: The team switches production to the backup site on purpose to prove it works. What type of test is this?
w: A failover test actually moves operations to the alternate system.
h: Flip the switch for real.

q: What does the recovery point objective (RPO) define?
o: Maximum acceptable data loss, in time
Average time to repair a system
w: RPO tells you how often backups must happen.
h: RPO = how much data you can lose.

q: What does the recovery time objective (RTO) define?
w: RTO is the deadline for restoring service.
h: RTO = how long you can be down.

q: Why aren't storage snapshots a full replacement for backups?
o: They often live on the same storage they protect
They can't be restored to a different system
They're always encrypted with the same key
They take far too long to create each day
w: A snapshot on the same array dies with the array or with an attacker who reaches it.
h: A snapshot in the same box isn't a backup.

q: Why encrypt backups that are sent offsite?
o: To protect data if the media is lost or stolen
To make restores from offsite media faster
To compress the backups to save space
To guarantee the RTO will be met
w: Offsite backups leave your control, so they need protection at rest.
h: If the tape gets lost, the data stays locked.

q: Only one admin knows how to restore the core banking system. Which resilience area needs work?
w: People are a resilience dependency too.
h: Don't let one person be the single point of failure.

q: The organization runs critical services on two different operating systems so one flaw can't take down everything. What is this?
w: Diversity avoids a single shared weakness.
h: Different platforms, different weak spots.

q: Under GDPR, what is the person whose personal data is processed called?
w: The data subject is the individual the data is about.
h: The subject is the person in the data.

q: Under GDPR, how quickly must a controller generally notify the supervisory authority of a qualifying breach?
w: GDPR sets a 72-hour notification window.
h: GDPR = 72 hours.

q: A form collects only the data needed for a loan application and nothing extra. Which privacy principle is this?
w: Collect only what you need.
h: Less data, less risk.

q: Data collected for loan processing is later used for unrelated marketing without consent. Which principle is violated?
w: Data should only be used for the purposes it was collected for.
h: Use it only for what you said.

q: Before launching a new app that collects member location data, the team assesses privacy risks. What is this?
w: A PIA identifies and reduces privacy risks before launch.
h: Check privacy before you build.

q: Names are replaced with codes, but a separate key can map them back. What is this?
w: Pseudonymized data can be re-identified, so it's still personal data.
h: Pseudo = it can come back.

q: Data is altered so it can never be linked back to any person. What is this?
w: Truly anonymized data is no longer personal data under GDPR.
h: Anonymous = gone for good.

q: Which is an example of personally identifiable information (PII)?
o: A member's name with their SSN
A public list of loan rates
w: PII identifies a specific person.
h: PII points to a person.

q: Which is protected health information (PHI)?
o: A patient's diagnosis linked to their name
w: PHI is health data tied to an identifiable person.
h: Health + identity = PHI.

q: Under GDPR, what is required for valid consent?
o: Freely given, specific, informed, and withdrawable
A one-time signature that can't be withdrawn
w: Consent must be a clear, active choice that can be taken back.
h: Consent is a clear yes that can become a no.

q: Which role advises an organization on GDPR compliance and is the contact for regulators?
w: The DPO oversees data protection compliance.
h: The DPO is the privacy referee inside the company.

q: Which document sets how long each type of personal data is kept before deletion?
w: Retention policies limit how long data is stored.
h: Keep it only as long as needed.

q: A member asks for a copy of all personal data the company holds about them. What is this request?
w: The right of access lets people see their data.
h: "Show me what you have on me."

q: What tells people what personal data is collected, why, and how it's used?
w: A privacy notice provides transparency to individuals.
h: The privacy notice says it upfront.

q: Developers need realistic data for testing but must not see real member information. What is BEST?
o: Use masked or synthetic test data
w: Test environments shouldn't hold real personal data.
h: Test with fakes, not with members.

q: What is the main purpose of a SIEM?
o: Collect and correlate logs to detect threats
Encrypt log files stored on each server
Block malware on endpoints in real time
Store backups of logs for compliance only
w: A SIEM aggregates logs and finds patterns across them.
h: SIEM sees the whole picture from many cameras.

q: What does a SOAR platform add on top of a SIEM?
w: SOAR automates repetitive response steps.
h: SIEM finds it; SOAR acts on it.

q: The SOC gets 2,000 alerts a day, mostly harmless. What should be done?
o: Tune alert rules to cut false positives
w: Alert tuning keeps analysts focused on real threats.
h: Too many alarms means none get heard.

q: How long should security logs be kept?
o: As long as policy and regulations require
Only until the next audit is complete
Until the server's disk is full
w: Retention is set by legal, regulatory, and investigative needs.
h: Keep logs as long as the rules say.

q: Which Windows Security Event ID records a successful logon?
w: 4624 is success, 4625 is failure.
h: 4624: in the door.

q: Which Windows Security Event ID records a failed logon?
w: Many 4625s can mean brute force or spraying.
h: 4625: door stayed shut.

q: Which Windows Security Event ID shows special privileges assigned to a new logon?
w: 4672 appears when an admin-level account logs on.
h: 4672: admin powers granted.

q: Logs are gathered by software installed on each server. What collection method is this?
w: Agents run on the host and forward logs.
h: Agent = software on the box.

q: A tool learns each user's normal behavior and alerts when an account acts very differently. What is it?
w: User and entity behavior analytics detect anomalies from baselines.
h: UEBA knows your habits.

q: A SIEM rule alerts on 10 failed logins followed by a success from the same IP. What is it detecting?
w: Correlating failures with a later success suggests a guessed password.
h: Fail, fail, fail, success = guessed.

q: Old logs move to low-cost, write-once storage for long-term keeping. What is this?
w: Archiving keeps logs affordable and tamper-resistant.
h: Archive the old, keep it safe.

q: A switch sends an immediate message to the monitoring server when a port goes down. What is this?
w: Traps are device-initiated alerts.
h: A trap is the device calling you.

q: Which log source shows which websites users visited?
w: Proxies record users' web requests.
h: The proxy saw every site.

q: Which log shows which device had a specific IP address at a given time?
w: DHCP leases map IPs to devices over time.
h: DHCP knows who had the address.

q: How do you protect logs from being altered by an attacker who controls a server?
o: Forward them to a central SIEM right away
Keep them only on the local server
Compress them on the local disk
Rotate them daily on the server
w: Copies outside the attacker's reach preserve integrity.
h: Send the logs somewhere the attacker can't reach.

q: Where should a network DLP appliance go to catch sensitive data leaving the organization?
w: DLP needs to see outbound traffic before it leaves.
h: Guard the exit.

q: Where does an email security gateway belong?
o: Between the internet and the mail server
After the mail server, facing users
w: It scans incoming mail before it reaches the mail server.
h: Check the mail at the mailbox, before it's delivered.

q: Where should a jump server be placed?
w: The jump server is the controlled door into management access.
h: The jump server lives in the admin hallway.

q: How should traffic between the user VLAN and the server VLAN be controlled?
o: An internal firewall enforcing rules between them
No controls since both are internal
w: Internal segmentation limits lateral movement.
h: Inside isn't automatically trusted.

q: Where is a VPN concentrator typically placed?
o: In the DMZ, behind the perimeter firewall
Outside the perimeter firewall with no protection
w: It faces remote users but should still be protected.
h: Edge-facing, but behind the wall.

q: Where is EDR installed?
w: EDR is an agent that watches activity on each host.
h: EDR lives on the device.

q: Internal web apps must be published to the internet without exposing the servers directly. What goes in the DMZ?
w: A reverse proxy accepts outside requests and forwards them inward.
h: The reverse proxy greets visitors at the door.

q: Where should an IDS sensor connect to see traffic between the core and the data center?
o: A SPAN port or tap on the core/data center link
The internet side of the modem only
w: Sensors must sit where the traffic flows.
h: Watch where the traffic actually passes.

q: A payment system's inline security device must stop all traffic if it fails, since security matters more than uptime. Which mode?
w: Fail-closed favors security over availability.
h: Fail-closed: when in doubt, block.

q: Where should guest devices be placed on the network?
o: A separate guest VLAN, internet only
The employee VLAN, with a warning
w: Guests should never share segments with internal systems.
h: Guests stay in the lobby.

q: Which option gives a complete, reliable copy of traffic even under heavy load?
w: SPAN ports can drop packets when busy; taps copy everything.
h: A tap copies every packet.

q: Where should the database server for a public website be placed?
o: On the internal network, not the DMZ
In the DMZ next to the web server
w: Only the web tier faces the internet; data stays deeper inside.
h: The web server is in the lobby; the vault is in back.

q: Where should a forward proxy for user web filtering be placed?
o: In front of public web servers
w: It intercepts users' outbound web traffic.
h: Forward proxy sits on the users' way out.

q: Where should an inline IPS sit relative to the perimeter firewall?
o: Outside the firewall, facing the internet
w: Behind the firewall, the IPS only inspects traffic the firewall already allowed.
h: Let the firewall sweep first, then inspect.

q: All of a remote user's traffic, including internet browsing, goes through the corporate VPN. What is this?
w: Full tunnel lets the company inspect all traffic.
h: Full tunnel: everything goes home first.

q: Only traffic for corporate resources goes through the VPN; other internet traffic goes direct. What is this?
w: Split tunneling saves bandwidth but bypasses corporate inspection.
h: Split: work through the tunnel, the rest goes direct.

q: What is the main security risk of split tunneling?
o: The VPN can no longer use MFA
The VPN must switch to IPsec
w: Users' direct internet traffic isn't filtered by the company.
h: What skips the tunnel skips the guards.

q: Two branch offices connect their networks through a permanent encrypted link. What is this?
w: Site-to-site VPNs connect whole networks.
h: Site-to-site links buildings.

q: A teleworker connects from a laptop to the corporate network. What type of VPN is this?
w: Remote access VPNs connect individual devices.
h: Remote access connects one person.

q: Why do TLS (SSL) VPNs connect easily through hotel and airport firewalls?
o: They use port 443, which is rarely blocked
They don't encrypt, so firewalls ignore them
They use UDP 500, which is always open
They bypass authentication on the firewall
w: HTTPS traffic is rarely blocked.
h: It looks like normal web traffic.

q: A contractor reaches an internal app through a web browser with no VPN software installed. What is this?
w: Clientless VPNs use the browser as the client.
h: No client, just a browser.

q: A laptop's VPN connects automatically before the user even logs in. What is this?
w: Always-on keeps devices connected and managed.
h: Always on, always protected.

q: Users work in desktops hosted in the data center, so member data never lands on their home PCs. What is this?
w: Virtual desktop infrastructure keeps data in the data center.
h: The data stays home; only the picture travels.

q: Which is the BEST way to give remote admins RDP access?
o: A shared admin account for RDP
w: A gateway wraps RDP in HTTPS and adds authentication controls.
h: Never expose RDP directly.

q: The VPN checks a laptop's patch level and antivirus before allowing the connection. What is this?
w: Posture checks keep unhealthy devices off the network.
h: Health check at the door.

q: Why require MFA on the VPN?
o: A stolen password alone can't connect
It removes the need for logging
w: MFA blocks attackers who only have credentials.
h: Password plus something else.

q: Why do mobile users benefit from IKEv2 VPNs?
w: IKEv2's MOBIKE support handles moving between Wi-Fi and cellular.
h: IKEv2 follows you between networks.

q: What helps if a remote user walks away with an open VPN session?
w: Timeouts close unattended sessions.
h: Walk away, get logged out.

q: Member records sit in a database on a server's disk. Which data state is this?
w: Stored data is at rest.
h: At rest = sitting still.

q: Member records travel from a branch to the core system over the WAN. Which data state is this?
w: Data moving across a network is in transit.
h: In transit = on the road.

q: An application loads member records into memory to calculate interest. Which data state is this?
w: Data being processed in memory is in use.
h: In use = being worked on.

q: A statement shows only the last four digits of the account number. What technique is this?
w: Masking hides part of the data from view.
h: Masking hides most of it.

q: A credit union's proprietary loan-scoring formula is protected because it gives a business advantage. How is it classified?
w: Trade secrets are confidential business information.
h: Secret recipe = trade secret.

q: Branch hours and product rates posted on the website. How are they classified?
w: Public data can be shared freely.
h: Public = anyone may see it.

q: A drive-destruction vendor provides a document proving each drive was destroyed. What is it?
w: Certificates prove secure disposal for audits.
h: Paper proof the drive is gone.

q: A law requires member data to stay within the country. Which control helps enforce this?
w: Location controls keep data in approved regions.
h: Keep the data inside the borders.

q: Why doesn't degaussing work on SSDs?
o: SSDs use flash memory, not magnetic media
SSDs are always encrypted by default
SSDs can't be removed from the laptop
SSDs hold their data only while powered
w: Degaussers erase magnetic media; SSDs need crypto erase or destruction.
h: Magnets don't wipe flash.

q: An encrypted drive is sanitized by destroying its encryption key. What is this?
w: Without the key, the data is unreadable.
h: Lose the key, lose the data.

q: What is the main purpose of a data classification label?
o: It tells people how the data must be handled
It encrypts the data it's attached to
It schedules the data for deletion
It speeds up backups of that data
w: Classification drives handling, storage, and sharing rules.
h: The label tells you the rules.

q: Which is an example of regulated data?
w: Regulated data is subject to laws or industry rules.
h: If a rulebook covers it, it's regulated.

q: The member database is placed on its own network segment reachable only from the app servers. What data protection method is this?
w: Segmentation limits who can reach sensitive data.
h: Put the vault in its own room.

q: The "Everyone" group is removed from a share containing loan files. What protection method is this?
w: Tightening access rights protects the data.
h: Fewer hands on the files.

q: Why is a root CA usually kept offline?
o: To protect its private key, which everything else trusts
Because root CAs can't connect to networks
w: If the root key is stolen, the whole PKI is compromised.
h: Keep the master key in the vault.

q: What does a certificate signing request (CSR) contain?
o: The public key and subject details
w: The private key never leaves the requester.
h: Send the public half, keep the private half.

q: A browser warns that a site's certificate isn't trusted, though the name matches. What is the MOST likely reason?
w: A self-signed cert doesn't chain to a trusted CA.
h: Vouching for yourself doesn't count.

q: One certificate must cover www.example.com, mail.example.com, and vpn.example.com. Which field makes this possible?
w: The SAN lists every hostname the certificate covers.
h: SAN = the list of names.

q: How does a CRL differ from OCSP?
o: A CRL is a downloaded list; OCSP answers per cert
A CRL is real-time; OCSP is a downloaded list
A CRL issues certificates; OCSP revokes them
They are the same mechanism with different names
w: CRLs are periodic lists; OCSP gives status on demand.
h: CRL is the whole list; OCSP asks about one.

q: How does a browser trust a website's certificate?
o: It follows the chain up to a trusted root
It trusts any certificate that has a SAN
It checks that the site's IP is public
It trusts any key longer than 2048 bits
w: The chain of trust ends at a root in the browser's trust store.
h: Follow the chain to a root you trust.

q: Why do organizations use intermediate CAs?
o: So the root can stay offline
So certificates cost less to issue
So no root CA is required
w: If an intermediate is compromised, it can be revoked without replacing the root.
h: Intermediates take the risk so the root doesn't.

q: A web server's private key was stolen. What should happen to its certificate?
o: Revoke it and reissue with a new key
Keep using it until it expires
Renew it with the same key pair
Move the site to a new IP address
w: A compromised key means the certificate can no longer be trusted.
h: Stolen key, burn the certificate.

q: Some clients reject a server's certificate with chain errors, though the cert itself is valid. What is the MOST likely cause?
o: The server isn't sending the intermediate
w: Servers must present the intermediate so clients can build the chain.
h: A missing link breaks the chain.

q: Users suddenly get certificate warnings on the VPN portal every morning starting today. What should be checked FIRST?
w: An expired certificate is the most common cause of sudden warnings.
h: Check the date first.

q: What signs a certificate to make it trustworthy?
w: The CA signs with its private key; clients verify with the CA's public key.
h: The CA signs; everyone checks with its public key.

q: Where do browsers and operating systems keep the root certificates they trust?
w: The trust store is the list of roots that anchor every chain.
h: The trust store is the list of who you trust.

q: When should an internal CA be used instead of a public CA?
w: Internal CAs are fine for devices and apps under your control.
h: Inside use, inside CA.

q: An employee is terminated. What should happen to their accounts?
w: Prompt deprovisioning stops former staff from keeping access.
h: Last day of work, last day of access.

q: Before creating an account, HR verifies a new hire's government ID. What is this?
w: Identity proofing confirms a person is who they claim before issuing credentials.
h: Prove who you are before you get a badge.

q: Employees of a partner company log in to your portal using their own company's credentials. What makes this possible?
w: Federation is trust between identity systems of different organizations.
h: Your ID works at the partner's door.

q: Which protocol adds an authentication layer with an ID token on top of OAuth 2.0?
w: OAuth handles authorization; OIDC adds identity.
h: OIDC = OAuth plus "who are you."

q: Which protocol queries a directory such as Active Directory, by default on port 389?
w: LDAP reads and searches directory data; LDAPS uses 636.
h: LDAP looks things up in the directory.

q: In SAML single sign-on, which party authenticates the user and issues the assertion?
w: The IdP vouches for the user; the SP trusts that assertion.
h: IdP says who you are; SP lets you in.

q: Which standard automates creating and removing user accounts in SaaS apps from a central identity system?
w: SCIM handles cross-domain provisioning and deprovisioning.
h: SCIM syncs accounts automatically.

q: New tellers automatically get the group memberships defined for the teller role. What is this?
w: Role templates make provisioning consistent and least-privilege.
h: Same job, same starter kit.

q: Which ports does RADIUS use for authentication and accounting?
w: RADIUS uses UDP 1812/1813; TACACS+ uses TCP 49.
h: RADIUS 1812, TACACS+ 49.

q: Kerberos logins fail on a server whose clock is 10 minutes off. Why?
o: Kerberos only works on Linux servers
DNS is blocking Kerberos on UDP 53
w: Kerberos tickets are time-stamped; too much clock skew causes failures.
h: Kerberos needs everyone's watches in sync.

q: When an employee leaves, why disable the account first instead of deleting it right away?
o: To keep audit history while blocking access
Because deleted accounts can't be recreated
So the user can still log in if needed
To save on licensing for that account
w: Disabling stops access but preserves records for investigations and handoffs.
h: Lock it first, delete it later.

q: With SAML, a user's account in a SaaS app is created automatically the first time they sign in. What is this?
w: JIT provisioning creates accounts on demand from the assertion.
h: The account appears when you first arrive.

q: What is the purpose of IKE Phase 1?
o: Authenticate the peers and build the IKE SA
Encrypt user data with the final session keys
Assign tunnel IP addresses to each peer
Negotiate NAT rules between the two peers
w: Phase 1 sets up the protected channel used to negotiate Phase 2.
h: Phase 1 builds the secure meeting room.

q: What does IKE Phase 2 (quick mode) negotiate?
o: The IPsec SAs that protect the data
The routing table entries for the tunnel
The DNS records for each peer
w: Phase 2 creates the SAs used for traffic.
h: Phase 2 sets up the data lanes.

q: How does IKEv1 aggressive mode differ from main mode?
o: It uses fewer messages but exposes identities
It uses more messages and more security
w: Aggressive mode is faster but less protected.
h: Aggressive: faster, but shows its ID.

q: What does ESP in tunnel mode protect?
o: The whole original packet, header included
Only the payload, not the original header
Only the original IP header, not the payload
w: Tunnel mode wraps the whole packet inside a new one.
h: Tunnel mode hides the whole car.

q: When is IPsec transport mode typically used?
o: Host-to-host, such as between two servers
Client-to-AP, such as for Wi-Fi logins
w: Transport mode protects the payload between two endpoints.
h: Transport = end to end, no new header.

q: What does the Security Parameter Index (SPI) do in IPsec?
o: Identifies which SA a packet uses
w: The SPI tells the receiver which SA to use.
h: SPI is the SA's ID tag.

q: Why use certificates instead of pre-shared keys for IPsec peer authentication across 50 sites?
o: Certificates scale better and can be revoked individually
Certificates remove the need for encryption
w: Managing one shared key across many sites is risky and hard to rotate.
h: Many sites, use certificates.

q: What is an advantage of IKEv2 over IKEv1?
o: Fewer messages, built-in NAT-T, and mobility
It drops encryption to improve speed
It requires AH for every tunnel
w: IKEv2 is simpler and more resilient.
h: IKEv2 is faster and handles movement.

q: An IPsec tunnel between two firewalls fails in Phase 1. What is the MOST likely cause?
o: Mismatched Phase 1 settings or pre-shared key
A missing DNS record for the peer
Too many users on the tunnel
The wrong SSID on the firewall
w: Both peers must agree on Phase 1 parameters and credentials.
h: Both sides must speak the same settings.

q: Testers get no information about the target before starting. What type of test is this?
w: Unknown environment testing simulates an outside attacker.
h: No map, no hints.

q: Testers receive network diagrams, source code, and credentials before starting. What type of test is this?
w: Full knowledge allows deep, efficient testing.
h: Full map in hand.

q: Testers receive only a list of IP ranges and one user account. What type of test is this?
w: Some information is shared, but not everything.
h: Half the map.

q: Which team plays the attacker during a security exercise?
w: The red team attacks; the blue team defends.
h: Red attacks.

q: Which team defends and responds during a security exercise?
w: The blue team monitors, detects, and responds.
h: Blue defends.

q: Attackers and defenders work together and share findings in real time to improve detection. What is this?
w: Purple mixes red and blue to improve defenses together.
h: Red + blue = purple.

q: After compromising a web server, a tester uses it to reach internal systems that weren't reachable before. What is this?
w: Pivoting uses a compromised host as a stepping stone.
h: Pivot off the first foothold.

q: A tester creates a scheduled task so access survives a reboot. What is this?
w: Persistence keeps access over time.
h: Persistence = staying in.

q: What must testers do at the end of a penetration test?
o: Remove their tools, accounts, and changes
Leave backdoors for next year's test
Delete the client's logs of the test
Keep copies of client data as proof
w: Cleanup returns systems to their original state.
h: Leave no trace of the test.
